posts.quote: I hid a spare key so I'd never get locked out. I hid it so well I've now been locked out twice, standing in the yard, guessing.
posts.caption: The fake rock was too obvious, so in April I got clever. That was my first mistake. I remember standing on the porch thinking nobody in a million years would look there, and I was right, because nobody now includes me. Last Tuesday at 6:40 I was in the front yard in my work shoes, lifting a ceramic frog, two flowerpots and a very offended gnome while the neighbor pretended to check his mail for nine straight minutes. It was under none of them. My sister finally texted me where I'd told her it was. The birdhouse. I had completely forgotten we own a birdhouse.
posts.first: My mother kept her spare key in a coffee can in the garage for thirty-one years and never once forgot where it was. I have tried four hiding spots since spring. The current one is a secret even from me, which my husband says is the whole point of hiding it. It is not.

posts.quote: Don't tell me to relax. I'm relaxed. This is just what my face does when you talk.
posts.caption: At my cousin's Labor Day cookout, a man I had known for eleven minutes told me to relax. I was holding a paper plate of potato salad and minding my own business by the cooler. Apparently my face was doing something. I have had this face for fifty-four years. It has been through two kitchen remodels, a wedding, and a timeshare presentation, and it has never once been asked to change. I explained this to him calmly. He went to go stand by the grill. My face, for the record, was perfectly relaxed the entire time he walked away.
posts.first: My mother had the same face and used it at church potlucks with tremendous results. People brought her extra deviled eggs just to stay on her good side. I inherited the face but not the eggs. I'm still working on that part.

posts.quote: I raked the leaves once in 1998. The wind has been handling it ever since.
posts.caption: There's a rake in my garage that I bought at a Sears that doesn't exist anymore. I used it one Saturday in October of 1998, made three beautiful piles, and watched a single gust of wind put every leaf back exactly where it started. I took that personally for about an hour. Then I took it as advice. Every fall since, the neighbors rake and bag and haul, and every spring my yard looks exactly like theirs. Nobody can tell the difference. The maple doesn't care either way. This year I've put a chair where the piles used to go.
posts.first: My neighbor Dale bought a leaf blower last week that sounds like a small airplane. He was out there Sunday at eight in the morning. By noon half his leaves were in my yard and I still hadn't done a thing. I consider that a partnership.

posts.quote: I bought three bags of Halloween candy early so I'd be ready. I was not ready. I'm on my fourth bag and it isn't even Halloween.
posts.first: The first bag lasted until a Thursday. I told myself I was testing it for quality, which is a real job somebody has to do. By the third bag I was hiding the wrappers at the bottom of the trash like a teenager. I am fifty-three years old.

posts.quote: At my age, getting ready mostly means finding the earrings that make people assume I tried.
posts.caption: Saturday night we had a dinner reservation at 7:30 and I started getting ready at 7:10. That's not confidence, that's math. Somewhere in my late forties I figured out that nobody looks at the outfit, nobody notices the shoes, and nobody has ever once asked about my mascara. They look at your ears. So I put on the same black top I always wear, pulled my hair into something, and spent eighteen of my twenty minutes finding the good gold hoops. Three different people told me I looked amazing. One asked if I'd done something new. I had. I'd found the earrings.
posts.first: My aunt Lorraine wore the same pair of pearl earrings to every wedding, funeral and bridge night for forty years. Everybody said she was the most put-together woman they knew. I asked her the secret once. She said nobody looks below the chin after sixty.

posts.quote: My idea of a girls' trip is all of us going to Target separately and texting pictures of the same throw pillow.
posts.caption: Four of us have been friends since 1989, and for about six years now we have been planning a trip to Savannah. There's a group chat for it. It has a name. Every spring somebody sends a link to a rental with a porch, everybody says yes, and every spring it quietly dies around the part where we pick dates. Meanwhile, last Thursday, all four of us ended up in four different stores in two states, and by 8 p.m. the chat had nineteen photos of the same mustard velvet pillow. Three of us bought it. That was the trip. It was a good one.
posts.first: I bought the pillow. It's on my armchair right now looking like it cost twice what it did. My friend Deb texted a picture of hers on her couch at the exact same moment. We didn't say a word about it. We didn't have to.

posts.quote: I bought a sweater that says 'Sweater Weather.' It's 81 degrees. I'm wearing it anyway. I've committed.
posts.caption: It was on the endcap the first week of October, cream-colored, chunky knit, little embroidered leaves across the front. I've been waiting since May for a reason to wear it. Then October did what October does around here and decided to be July again. I wore it to the farmers market Saturday anyway. By ten o'clock I was holding a jar of apple butter against my neck to cool down. A woman selling honey asked if I was okay. I said I was dressing for the season I was promised. She gave me a free sample. I'm fairly sure it was pity honey.
posts.first: My daughter saw the picture and asked why my face was so red. I told her it was an autumn glow. She said it looked more like a sunburn. She's not wrong, but she's also not invited to the next farmers market.

posts.quote: You don't have to like my casserole. You just have to stop taking seconds of it while you tell me.
posts.caption: My brother-in-law has had opinions about my green bean casserole since 2004. Too many onions. Not enough onions. Why is it orange. It's not orange, Gary, it's the lighting. Every holiday he gives me the full review out loud, at the table, to anyone sitting near him. And every holiday, somewhere around the second football game, I look up and he's back at the dish with a serving spoon, quietly going in for thirds. Last Easter he took the leftovers home in a whipped topping tub. I watched him do it. I have the receipts and I have the tub.
posts.first: My mother-in-law told me once that nobody complains about food they don't eat. I didn't understand it at the time. I understand it every Thanksgiving now, standing by the stove, watching that man scrape the corners of a dish he's been criticizing since the turkey went in.

posts.first: I woke up with the remote on my chest and the TV asking if I was still watching. I was not. Nobody was. My husband had covered me with a blanket and gone to bed. That's love at this age. A blanket and no questions.

posts.quote: I've stopped reading the terms and conditions. I've also stopped reading the room. Both have worked out fine.
posts.caption: My granddaughter set up a new streaming app on my TV last month, and a screen came up with forty-seven pages of terms. She asked if I wanted to read them. I said I've been agreeing to things without reading them since my first mortgage, and that turned out fine. Then at Sunday dinner my son-in-law started explaining his fantasy football league, and I asked if there was going to be a quiz. Apparently the room got a little quiet. I didn't notice. I was having a lovely time. We got the app working, by the way.
posts.first: I have clicked 'I agree' on so many things by now that I've probably signed my house over to three different software companies. Nobody has come to collect yet. If they do, they can wait until my show is over.

posts.quote: I don't do casual Friday. I do 'this is cashmere and I will not be helping you move.'
posts.caption: My friend Janet texted Thursday night asking what I was doing Saturday. Nobody asks what you're doing Saturday unless there's a couch involved. Sure enough, she was moving out of the townhouse, the truck was coming at nine, and could I possibly. I wrote back that I'd love to come by around four with a lasagna. She said that was after the heavy stuff. I said I know. I showed up at 4:05 in my good navy sweater, carried one box of throw pillows from the car to the porch, and got thanked like I'd moved the piano. Timing is everything.
posts.first: The year I turned fifty I made a rule that I don't lift anything heavier than a casserole dish for anyone I haven't known at least twenty years. Janet is at nineteen. She has until next spring. I've told her about the rule. She's counting.

posts.quote: I don't argue with people anymore. I just say 'you might be right' and let them live with the uncertainty.
posts.caption: Thirty years ago I would have stayed at a dinner party until midnight proving a point about which way the toilet paper goes. I had charts in my head. I had examples. These days, when somebody across the table tells me with total confidence that you can't freeze milk, I just look at them, nod slowly, and say, you might be right. Then I take a sip and change the subject. It eats at them. Last month a man called my husband two days later to ask if I'd actually agreed with him. My husband said he couldn't really say. That man is still thinking about it.
posts.first: My grandmother used to do this at the beauty parlor to whoever was under the dryer next to her. She'd say, well, you might be right, honey, and go back to her magazine. It took me forty years to realize that was the meanest thing she ever said to anyone.
